newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FORECAST-ABN AMRO year net seen up 26 pct.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-ABN AMRO year net seen up 26 pct.

text.p: Global bank ABN AMRO NV is set to report a 26 percent leap in annual net profit next Thursday on the back of buoyant financial markets and strong lending, and despite a slowing of growth in the second half, analysts said.
They said interest would be high in the Dutch group's hidden reserves, which will be unveiled for the first time with the results, and its policy on future loan provisions.
Forecasts of 1996 net profit range between 3.27 billion and 3.32 billion guilders, compared with 2.62 billion in 1995. The average forecast of 3.29 billion is 26 percent up on 1995.
"They've had very favourable trading conditions in all areas," said BZW Nederland analyst Heinie Hakker.
Net attributable profit is estimated at between 3.00 billion and 3.13 billion guilders, up from 2.37 billion a year earlier.
Earnings per share are seen at between 9.16 and 9.45 guilders, versus 7.69, with annual dividends expected to total between 3.80 and 4.25 guilders, from 3.60 in 1995.
The interim dividend was 1.80 guilders per share.
Daan Worm of ING Barings said he expected net profit growth to have slowed to 16 percent in the second half, from the 36 percent seen in the first half when markets were soaring.

"The second half of 1995 was a tougher comparison base," he said, adding however that financial markets and mergers and acquisitions activity in the second half of 1996 might have been healthier than originally thought.
He said share prices of Dutch financial stocks had outperformed the overall market since the start of the year, foreshadowing a possible profit surprise when they report.
Jacob Bosscha of Bank Labouchere said ABN AMRO would also have been helped by the strength of the dollar, which averaged 1.69 guilders in 1996 from 1.60 a year earlier.
A large proportion of the bank's income is dollar-based.
Hakker said ABN AMRO experienced good demand for loans and favourable securities markets in 1996, adding that interest rates were also in their favour.
Jean-Paul van Bavel of F. van Lanschot Bankiers forecast income growth of 11.5 percent from net interest, 16 percent from commissions and 34 percent from financial transactions.
"Everyone knows 1996 earnings will be good but there will be more focus on 1997," he said, referring to the impact of the announcement of the size of the hidden reserves.
Analysts have estimated the reserves, known as the provision for general risks (VAR), at 4.0-5.0 billion guilders.
Having built up the VAR in the past by overproviding for loan losses, the bank has indicated it will cut provisioning in future, but analysts are more interested in the extent.

Hakker said another important question was how much money ABN AMRO would provide for the costs of the new euro currency, the millennium and automation projects, after setting aside 100 million guilders in the first half.
"They showed in the first half they have flexibility in how they report expenses such as the euro and the year 2000," said Neil Crowder of Goldman Sachs.
